Entanglement of the Antisymmetric State

Matthias Christandl Affiliation: Institute for Theoretical Physics, ETH Zurich, 8093 Zurich, Switzerland Affiliation: Faculty of Physics, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Theresienstr. 37, 80333 Munich, Germany Email: christandl@phys.ethz.ch    Norbert Schuch Affiliation: Institute for Quantum Information, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena CA 91125, U.S.A. Affiliation: Max-Planck-Institut für Quantenoptik, Hans-Kopfermann-Str. 1, D-85748 Garching, Germany Email: norbert.schuch@googlemail.com    Andreas Winter Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, University of Bristol, Bristol BS8 1TW, U.K. Affiliation: Centre for Quantum Technologies, National University of Singapore, 2 Science Drive 3, Singapore 117542 Email: a.j.winter@bris.ac.uk
18 January 2011
Abstract

We analyse the entanglement of the antisymmetric state in dimension d×dd\times d and present two main results. First, we show that the amount of secrecy that can be extracted from the state is low, more precisely, the distillable key is bounded by O⁡(1d)O(\frac{1}{d}). Second, we show that the state is highly entangled in the sense that a large number of ebits are needed in order to create the state: entanglement cost is larger than a constant, independent of dd. The second result is shown to imply that the regularised relative entropy with respect to separable states is also lower bounded by a constant.

In order to prove the first result we show that for all states the squashed entanglement upper bounds the distillable key. Using the unitary symmetry of the antisymmetric state we are then able to bound the squashed entanglement. A symmetry argument is also used in the second bound, where the representation theory of the unitary group is employed in order to reduce a semi-definite programming relaxation of the entanglement cost of the antisymmetric states to a manageable linear program. Finally, we note that the regularised relative entropy of entanglement is asymptotically continuous in the state. The results in this paper have previously been announced in Phys. Rev. Lett. 104, 240405 (2010).

I Introduction

Entanglement is a quantum phenomenon governing the correlations between two quantum systems. It is both responsible for Einstein’s “spooky action at a distance” [1] as well as the security of quantum key distribution [2, 3]. Quantum key distribution, or QKD for short, is a procedure to distribute a perfectly secure key among two distant parties, something that is not possible in classical cryptography without assumptions on the eavesdropper.

In the early days of quantum information theory, it was quickly realised that the universal resource for bipartite entanglement is the ebit, that is, the state |ψ⟩:=12​(|00⟩+|11⟩)|\psi\rangle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|00\rangle+|11\rangle) [4]. Ebits are needed for teleportation [5], superdense coding [6] and directly lead to secret bits [3, 7]. It is therefore natural to associate the usefulness of a quantum state with the amount of ebits that can be extracted from it or the amount of ebits needed to create the state [8]. Formally, one considers the distillable entanglement

ED(ρ)=limϵ→0limn→∞supΛn​ LOCC{mn:∥Λn(ρ⊗n)−ψ⊗m∥1≤ϵ},E_{D}(\rho)=\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sup_{\Lambda_{n}\text{ LOCC}}\left\{\frac{m}{n}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\|\Lambda_{n}(\rho^{\otimes n})-\psi^{\otimes m}\|_{1}\leq\epsilon\right\}, (1)

and the entanglement cost

EC(ρ)=limϵ→0limn→∞infΛn​ LOCC{mn:∥Λn(ψ⊗m)−ρ⊗n∥1≤ϵ},E_{C}(\rho)=\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\inf_{\Lambda_{n}\text{ LOCC}}\left\{\frac{m}{n}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\|\Lambda_{n}(\psi^{\otimes m})-\rho^{\otimes n}\|_{1}\leq\epsilon\right\}, (2)

where the supremum and infimum ranges over all completely positive trace preserving (CPTP) maps that can be obtained from local operations and classical communication (LOCC) on the state. For ease of notation we write ψ\psi short for |ψ⟩​⟨ψ|.|\psi\rangle\!\langle\psi|.

An important result relating to these quantities has been the discovery of bound entanglement, that is of states that need ebits for their creation but from which no ebits can be extracted asymptotically: EC​(ρ)>0E_{C}(\rho)>0 and ED​(ρ)=0E_{D}(\rho)=0 [9]. A recent surprise has been the realization that there exist bound entangled states from which secrecy can be extracted [10], a result that overthrew previous beliefs that secrecy extraction and entanglement distillation would go hand in hand.

This has motivated research into the amount of key that can be distilled from a quantum state, in its own right. The distillable key is defined as

KD(ρA​B)=limϵ→0limn→∞supΛn​ LOCC,γm{mn:∥Λn(ρ⊗n)−γm∥1≤ϵ},K_{D}(\rho_{AB})=\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sup_{\Lambda_{n}\text{ LOCC},\gamma_{m}}\left\{\frac{m}{n}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\|\Lambda_{n}(\rho^{\otimes n})-\gamma_{m}\|_{1}\leq\epsilon\right\}, (3)

where γm\gamma_{m} denotes a quantum state which contains mm bits of pure secrecy (see Definition 4).

A fundamental question at this point is this. Do there exist states which require key to create them but from which no secret key can be distilled asymptotically? Even the weaker form, whether there exist states with EC​(ρ)>0E_{C}(\rho)>0 but KD​(ρ)=0K_{D}(\rho)=0, seems too difficult at the moment. Here we show that in an asymptotic sense the answer is yes: in the spirit of [11], we show that there exists a family of states with constant lower bound on their entanglement cost, but arbitrarily small distillable key.

In order to derive this result, we make use of the theory of entanglement with its many entanglement measures. The motivation for this is the following. Due to their asymptotic definitions it is a difficult task to evaluate the distillable entanglement, the entanglement cost and the distillable key on specific quantum states. They have in common that they measure the amount of entanglement in a quantum state, i.e. they do not increase under local operations and classical communication (LOCC), they vanish on separable states and they equal one when evaluated on an ebit. This has led to an axiomatisation of the quantities that measure entanglement and to the definition of a whole zoo of entanglement measures. One of the main uses of all the new entanglement measures is that they are mostly sandwiched between distillable entanglement (or even distillable key) and entanglement cost and hence form upper and lower bounds for these quantities. Even though these new entanglement measures often involve complicated minimisations or asymptotic limits they are sometimes easier to calculate than distillable entanglement, distillable key and entanglement cost.

The states for which entanglement measures have been calculated are typically characterised by their symmetry. The most prominent example are so-called Werner states in dimension 𝐂d⊗𝐂d\mathbf{C}^{d}\otimes\mathbf{C}^{d}, charaterised by the equation

(g⊗g)​ρ​(g†⊗g†)=ρ(g\otimes g)\rho(g^{\dagger}\otimes g^{\dagger})=\rho

for all g∈U⁡(d)g\in U(d), the unitary group. This family of states can be given explicitly as the one parameter family

ρ=p​σd+(1−p)​αd,\rho=p\sigma_{d}+(1-p)\alpha_{d},

where p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1] and σd\sigma_{d} is the state proportional to the projectors onto the symmetric subspace and αd\alpha_{d} is the state proportional to the projector onto the antisymmetric subspace. In this work we will bound the value of certain entanglement measures for the totally antisymmetric states αd\alpha_{d}.

The first entanglement measure we use is the squashed entanglement [12],

Es​q(ρA​B)=infρA​B​E:ρA​B=TrE⁡ρA​B​E12I(A;B|E)ρ,E_{sq}(\rho_{AB})=\inf_{\rho_{ABE}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\rho_{AB}=\operatorname{Tr}_{E}\rho_{ABE}}\frac{1}{2}I(A;B|E)_{\rho}, (4)

where I​(A;B|E)ρ=H​(A​E)ρ+H​(B​E)ρ−H​(A​B​E)ρ−H​(E)ρI(A;B|E)_{\rho}=H(AE)_{\rho}+H(BE)_{\rho}-H(ABE)_{\rho}-H(E)_{\rho} is the quantum conditional mutual information, with H​(X)ρ=H⁡(ρX)H(X)_{\rho}=H(\rho_{X}) the von Neumann entropy of the reduced state on XX, H⁡(σ):=−Tr⁡σ​log2​σH(\sigma)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=-\operatorname{Tr}\sigma\log_{2}\sigma. We show that it is an upper bound on the distillable key and hence establish the chain of inequalities

ED≤KD≤Es​q≤EC.E_{D}\leq K_{D}\leq E_{sq}\leq E_{C}. (5)

A concrete calculation of a bound on the squashed entanglement of the antisymmetric states will yield our first main result, an upper bound on the distillable key.

Theorem 1
KD​(αd)\displaystyle K_{D}(\alpha_{d}) ≤{log2⁡d+2d if ​d​ is even12​log2​d+3d−1 if ​d​ is odd}=O(1d).\displaystyle\leq\left.\begin{cases}\log_{2}\frac{d+2}{d}&\text{ if }d\text{ is even}\\ \frac{1}{2}\log_{2}\frac{d+3}{d-1}&\text{ if }d\text{ is odd}\end{cases}\right\}=O\left(\frac{1}{d}\right). (6)

In order to find a lower bound on the entanglement cost of the antisymmetric state, we will use its charaterisation as the regularised entanglement of formation EC=EF∞E_{C}=E_{F}^{\infty}. The entanglement of formation is defined as

EF(ρ)=min{pi,|φ⟩​⟨φ|i}i:ρ=∑ipi​|φi⟩​⟨φi|∑ipiH(TrB|φi⟩⟨φi|),E_{F}(\rho)=\min_{\{p_{i},|\varphi\rangle\!\langle\varphi|_{i}\}_{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\rho=\sum_{i}p_{i}|\varphi_{i}\rangle\!\langle\varphi_{i}|}\sum_{i}p_{i}H\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_{B}|\varphi_{i}\rangle\!\langle\varphi_{i}|\bigr), (7)

and its regularisation is given by

EC​(ρ)=EF∞​(ρ):=limn→∞1n​EF​(ρ⊗n).\displaystyle E_{C}(\rho)=E_{F}^{\infty}(\rho)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n}E_{F}\bigl(\rho^{\otimes n}\bigr). (8)

Making heavy use of the symmetry of the antisymmetric state we will relax the minimisation in the definition of the entanglement of formation to a linear programme and obtain the second main result of this paper.

Theorem 2

EC​(αd)≥log2⁡43≈0.415.\displaystyle{E_{C}(\alpha_{d})\geq\log_{2}\frac{4}{3}\approx 0.415.}

It is not difficult to see that the entanglement of formation of this state equals one and hence that the truth of the additivity conjecture for entanglement of formation would have implied EC​(αd)=1E_{C}(\alpha_{d})=1. Since Hastings has provided a counterexample [13] to the additivity conjecture [14], this consequence is put into doubt and the only evidence was Yura’s brute force calculation in dimension three, where he proved EC​(α3)=1E_{C}(\alpha_{3})=1. Our result can therefore be seen as supporting evidence for EC​(αd)=1E_{C}(\alpha_{d})=1, and at least provides a further example where some weak form of additivity holds. At present the techniques in this paper are not sufficient to prove EC​(αd)=1E_{C}(\alpha_{d})=1, but further development of them may be capable of doing so.

As a corollary to Theorem 2 we obtain a lower bound to the regularised relative entropy of entanglement with respect to separable states

Corollary 3

ER,sep∞​(αd)≥log2⁡43≈0.207.\displaystyle{E_{R,\mathrm{sep}}^{\infty}(\alpha_{d})\geq\log_{2}\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}}\approx 0.207.}

Here, the relative entropy of entanglement (with respect to separable states) is defined as

ER,sep(ρ):=minσ​separableD(ρ||σ),\displaystyle E_{R,\mathrm{sep}}(\rho)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\min_{\sigma\ \text{separable}}D(\rho||\sigma),

where D(ρ||σ):=Trρ[logρ−logσ]D(\rho||\sigma)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\operatorname{Tr}\rho[\log\rho-\log\sigma], and the regularised relative entropy of entanglement is

ER,sep∞​(ρ)=limn→∞1n​ER,sep​(ρ⊗n).\displaystyle E_{R,\mathrm{sep}}^{\infty}(\rho)=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\tfrac{1}{n}E_{R,\mathrm{sep}}(\rho^{\otimes n}). (9)

From the point of view of entanglement theory, this result is interesting for at least three reasons. First, it shows that the additivity violation of the relative entropy of entanglement for the antisymmetric state, first observed in [15], is not very strong in the asymptotic limit. Secondly, the regularised relative entropy of entanglement with respect to separable states behaves very differently to the relative entropy of entanglement with respect to PPT states, as the latter takes the value log2⁡d+2d\log_{2}\frac{d+2}{d} [16]. Thirdly, it shows that the relative entropy of entanglement can sometimes be larger and sometimes be smaller than the squashed entanglement. Finally, we note that as an entanglement measure, the relative entropy of entanglement with respect to separable states satisfies [10]

ED≤KD≤ER,sep∞≤EC.E_{D}\leq K_{D}\leq E_{R,\mathrm{sep}}^{\infty}\leq E_{C}.

and that it is asymptotically continuous, as we show in Proposition 14.

In order to derive both main results of the paper we make use of the symmetry properties of the antisymmetric state and the associated representation theory of the unitary group in dimension dd. For the lower bound on entanglement cost, we relax the calculation of EF​(αd⊗n)E_{F}(\alpha_{d}^{\otimes n}) in a first step into a semidefinite programme which we reduce in a second step with the help of representation theory (for the first time using the concept of a plethysm in quantum information theory) into a linear programme [17]. We then find a feasible point of the dual for the latter, which results in our lower bound of log2⁡43\log_{2}\frac{4}{3} for entanglement cost. On the way we recover Yura’s result for d=3d=3.

The rest of the paper is organised as follows. In Section II we introduce the notation from representation theory that will be used throughout the paper. In Section III we prove the upper bound on the squashed entanglement and distillable key. In Section IV we exhibit the sequence of relaxations that will lead to the lower bound on the entanglement cost. In Section V we will derive the lower bound on regularised relative entropy of entanglement of the antisymmetric state with respect to separable states. Furthermore, we establish that it is asymptotically continuous as a function of the state. We will conclude the paper with remarks and open questions in Section VI. The appendices contain details on the representation-theoretic calculations and the linear programme, which have been omitted in the main text.

II Representation theoretic preliminaries

Representations of the unitary group U⁡(d)U(d) can be taken to be unitary and decompose into a direct sum of irreducible representations. The latter are classified according to their highest weight. For each dominant weight λ\lambda, i.e. λ=(λ1,…,λd)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d}) with λi≥λi+1∈𝐙\lambda_{i}\geq\lambda_{i+1}\in{\bf Z} there is exactly one irreducible representation VλV_{\lambda}. When λd≥0\lambda_{d}\geq 0, we write λ⊢dn\lambda\vdash_{d}n if n:=|λ|:=∑iλin\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=|\lambda|\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}. Such VλV_{\lambda} can be viewed as a subrepresentations of the nn-fold diagonal action of the unitary group on (𝐂d)⊗n(\mathbf{C}^{d})^{\otimes n}:

Tn:g↦g⊗n,T^{n}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}g\mapsto g^{\otimes n},

since by Schur-Weyl duality

Tn≅⨁λ⊢dnVλ⊗𝐂dim[λ],T^{n}\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash_{d}n}V_{\lambda}\otimes\mathbf{C}^{\dim[\lambda]},

where [λ][\lambda] denotes the SnS_{n}-Specht module corresponding to the Young frame λ\lambda. In the following we will often use the interpretation of λ\lambda as a Young frame, i.e. as a diagram of boxes arranged in dd rows with λi\lambda_{i} boxes in row ii, and use the corresponding diagrammatic notation. As a vector space, VλV_{\lambda} can be constructed as the image of the Young symmetriser, a certain element in the group algebra of SnS_{n}, when applied to (𝐂d)⊗n(\mathbf{C}^{d})^{\otimes n}. The projector onto VλV_{\lambda} is denoted by PλP_{\lambda}.

Two types of representations are of particular importance. First, the symmetric representations with Young diagram λ=(n,0,…,0)\lambda=(n,0,\ldots,0) which act on the totally symmetric subspace Symn​(𝐂d)\mathrm{Sym}^{n}(\mathbf{C}^{d}) of (𝐂d)⊗n(\mathbf{C}^{d})^{\otimes n}. Second, the fundamental representations with Young diagram λ=(1,1,…,1,0,0,…,0)\lambda=(1,1,\ldots,1,0,0,\ldots,0) which act on the totally antisymmetric subspace ∧n(𝐂d)\wedge^{n}(\mathbf{C}^{d}) of (𝐂d)⊗n(\mathbf{C}^{d})^{\otimes n}. Note that the latter are zero-dimensional for d<nd<n.

The dimension of VλV_{\lambda} is given by Weyl’s dimension formula

dimVλ=∏i<j(λi−λj−i+j)∏k=1d−1k!\displaystyle\dim V_{\lambda}=\frac{\prod_{i<j}(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j}-i+j)}{\prod_{k=1}^{d-1}k!} (10)

and specializes in the case of a fundamental representation to (dn)\binom{d}{n}.

The first case of interest to us is n=2n=2, where

T2≅V(1,1)⊕V(2,0),T^{2}\cong V_{(1,1)}\oplus V_{(2,0)},

or in diagrammatic notation

III Upper bound on the distillable key

In this section we will first show that squashed entanglement is an upper bound to the amount of key that one can distill from quantum states. Then we will find an upper bound on squashed entanglement of the antisymmetric state. Together, this proves Theorem 1.

Recall the definition of squashed entanglement and the definition of the key rate. The latter contains a maximisation over states that contain at least mm bits of secrecy, the formal definition of such states follows.

Definition 4 ([10])

A private state containing at least mm bits of secrecy is a state γm\gamma_{m} of the form

γm=U​σA​A′​B​B′​U†\gamma_{m}=U\sigma_{AA^{\prime}BB^{\prime}}U^{\dagger}

for some unitary U=∑i|i​i⟩​⟨i​i|⊗UiU=\sum_{i}|ii\rangle\!\langle ii|\otimes U_{i} and σA​A′​B​B′=ΦA​B⊗σA′​B′\sigma_{AA^{\prime}BB^{\prime}}=\Phi_{AB}\otimes\sigma_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}}, where |Φ⟩=12m​∑i=12m|i⟩​|i⟩|\Phi\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{m}}}\sum_{i=1}^{2^{m}}|i\rangle|i\rangle is the maximally entangled state of rank 2m2^{m}. System A​BAB is known as the key part of the state and system A′​B′A^{\prime}B^{\prime} is known as the shield part.

Lemma 5

For all bipartite quantum states ρA​B\rho_{AB},

KD​(ρA​B)≤Es​q​(ρA​B).K_{D}(\rho_{AB})\leq E_{sq}(\rho_{AB}).
Proof.

Let Λn\Lambda_{n} be an LOCC protocol given by a CPTP map Λn\Lambda_{n} with

‖Λn​(ρ⊗n)−γm‖1≤ϵ\|\Lambda_{n}(\rho^{\otimes n})-\gamma_{m}\|_{1}\leq\epsilon

and assume that the dimension of the A′​B′A^{\prime}B^{\prime} part is at most exponential in nn. This last assumption can be made without loss of generality since the optimal key distillation protocol can be approximated by a sequence of protocols satisfying this requirement. In order to see this, note that one can stop the optimal protocol when the extracted bits are almost perfect and use privacy amplification to make them perfect. Privacy amplification only needs an amount of communication that is linear in the amount of bits extracted. Therefore, without loss of generality, the dimension the shield size can be assumed to grow at most exponentially in nn.

Since squashed entanglement is a monotone under LOCC [12] and asymptotically continuous [18]

Es​q​(ρ⊗n)≥Es​q​(Λ⁡(ρ⊗n))≥Es​q​(γm)−16​c​ϵ​n​log2​d−4​h​(2​ϵ),E_{sq}(\rho^{\otimes n})\geq E_{sq}(\Lambda(\rho^{\otimes n}))\geq E_{sq}(\gamma_{m})-16c\sqrt{\epsilon}n\log_{2}d-4h(2\sqrt{\epsilon}),

where cc is the constant relating to the shield size. Recall from Definition 4 the form of the state γm\gamma_{m}. In order to show that Es​q​(γm)≥mE_{sq}(\gamma_{m})\geq m, consider an extension σA​A′​B​B′​E\sigma_{AA^{\prime}BB^{\prime}E} of σA​A′​B​B′\sigma_{AA^{\prime}BB^{\prime}} and the induced extension γA​A′​B​B′​E=U⊗𝟙𝔼​σ𝔸​𝔸′​𝔹​𝔹′​𝔼​𝕌†⊗𝟙𝔼\gamma_{AA^{\prime}BB^{\prime}E}=U\otimes\openone_{E}\,\sigma_{AA^{\prime}BB^{\prime}E}\,U^{\dagger}\otimes\openone_{E} of γA​A′​B​B′\gamma_{AA^{\prime}BB^{\prime}}. Clearly,

H​(A​A′​B​B′​E)γ=H​(A​A′​B​B′​E)σ=H​(A′​B′​E)σ=H​(A′​B′​E)σi,H(AA^{\prime}BB^{\prime}E)_{\gamma}=H(AA^{\prime}BB^{\prime}E)_{\sigma}=H(A^{\prime}B^{\prime}E)_{\sigma}=H(A^{\prime}B^{\prime}E)_{\sigma_{i}},

with σi:=Ui⊗𝟙𝔼​σ𝔸′​𝔹′​𝔼​𝕌𝕚†⊗𝟙𝔼\sigma_{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=U_{i}\otimes\openone_{E}\sigma_{A^{\prime}B^{\prime}E}U_{i}^{\dagger}\otimes\openone_{E}. Furthermore

H​(E)σi=H​(E)ρandH​(A​A′​E)γ=H​(A)γ+∑ipi​H​(A′​E)σiH(E)_{\sigma_{i}}=H(E)_{\rho}\quad\textrm{and}\quad H(AA^{\prime}E)_{\gamma}=H(A)_{\gamma}+\sum_{i}p_{i}H(A^{\prime}E)_{\sigma_{i}}

and similarly for H​(B​B′​E)γH(BB^{\prime}E)_{\gamma}. Altogether this gives

I​(A​A′;B​B′|E)γ≥H​(A)γ+H​(B)γ+∑ipi​I​(A′;B′|E)σi≥2​m,I(AA^{\prime};BB^{\prime}|E)_{\gamma}\geq H(A)_{\gamma}+H(B)_{\gamma}+\sum_{i}p_{i}I(A^{\prime};B^{\prime}|E)_{\sigma_{i}}\geq 2m,

where the non-negativity of the quantum mutual information was used in the last inequality. This shows that Es​q​(γm)≥mE_{sq}(\gamma_{m})\geq m and therefore Es​q​(ρ)≥mn−16​c​ϵ​log2​d−4n​h​(2​ϵ)E_{sq}(\rho)\geq\frac{m}{n}-16c\sqrt{\epsilon}\log_{2}d-\frac{4}{n}h(2\sqrt{\epsilon}), with the RHS converging to KD​(ρA​B)K_{D}(\rho_{AB}).   ⊓\sqcap⊔\sqcup

The following lemma provides an upper bound on the squashed entanglement of the antisymmetric state.

Lemma 6

For even dd, we have

Es​q​(αd)≤log2⁡d+2d.E_{sq}(\alpha_{d})\leq\log_{2}\frac{d+2}{d}.

For odd dd,

Es​q​(αd)≤12​log2​d+3d−1.E_{sq}(\alpha_{d})\leq\frac{1}{2}\log_{2}\frac{d+3}{d-1}.
Proof.

Let PkP_{k} be the projector onto the ∧k(𝐂d)\wedge^{k}(\mathbf{C}^{d}) in (𝐂d)⊗k(\mathbf{C}^{d})^{\otimes k}. Recall that dk:=dim∧k(𝐂d)=(dk)d_{k}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\dim\wedge^{k}(\mathbf{C}^{d})=\binom{d}{k} and define ρA​B​E:=Pkdk\rho_{ABE}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\frac{P_{k}}{d_{k}}, where ℋA≅ℋB≅𝐂d{\cal H}_{A}\cong{\cal H}_{B}\cong\mathbf{C}^{d} correspond to the first and the second tensor factor and ℋE≅(𝐂d)⊗k−2{\cal H}_{E}\cong(\mathbf{C}^{d})^{\otimes k-2} to the last k−2k-2 factors. It is clear that the reduced density matrix ρA​B:=TrE⁡ρA​B​E\rho_{AB}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\operatorname{Tr}_{E}\rho_{ABE} equals the totally antisymmetric state αd\alpha_{d}, or conversely, that ρA​B​E\rho_{ABE} is an extension of αd\alpha_{d}. For this extension we evaluate the conditional mutual information:

I​(A;B|E)ρ=H​(A​E)ρ+H​(B​E)ρ−H​(E)ρ−H​(A​B​E)ρ=log2⁡dk−12dk−2​dk=log2⁡kk−1​d−k+2d−k+1.I(A;B|E)_{\rho}=H(AE)_{\rho}+H(BE)_{\rho}-H(E)_{\rho}-H(ABE)_{\rho}=\log_{2}\frac{d_{k-1}^{2}}{d_{k-2}d_{k}}=\log_{2}\frac{k}{k-1}\frac{d-k+2}{d-k+1}.

Minimising this function over different values of k∈{2,…,d}k\in\{2,\ldots,d\} we find that for even dd the minimum value I​(A;B|E)ρ=2​log2​d+2dI(A;B|E)_{\rho}=2\log_{2}\frac{d+2}{d} is reached when k=d2+1k=\frac{d}{2}+1 and for odd dd the minimum value I​(A;B|E)ρ=log2⁡d+3d−1I(A;B|E)_{\rho}=\log_{2}\frac{d+3}{d-1} is reached when k=d+12k=\frac{d+1}{2}.   ⊓\sqcap⊔\sqcup

It is surprising that the bound from Lemma 6 for even dimension coincides with values of other entanglement measures [16]:

ER,PPT∞​(αd)=ERains​(αd)=EN​(αd)=log2⁡d+2d,E_{R,\mathrm{PPT}}^{\infty}(\alpha_{d})=E_{\text{Rains}}(\alpha_{d})=E_{N}(\alpha_{d})=\log_{2}\frac{d+2}{d},

where ER,PPT∞E_{R,\mathrm{PPT}}^{\infty} is the regularised relative entropy of entanglement with respect to PPT states (a PPT state is a state whose partial transpose is a positive semidefinite operator), ERainsE_{\text{Rains}} is the Rains bound and ENE_{N} is the logarithmic negativity. In the light of these results we are tempted to conjecture that Es​q​(αd)=log2⁡d+2dE_{sq}(\alpha_{d})=\log_{2}\frac{d+2}{d}, at least for even dd.

With the upper bound on squashed entanglement we not only match the best known upper bounds on distillable entanglement (for even dimension) but obtain new bounds even on the distillable key, since Lemma 5 and Lemma 6 prove Theorem 1.

Note also that our bound gives Es​q​(αd)≤2​log2​ed−1=O⁡(1d)E_{sq}(\alpha_{d})\leq\frac{2\log_{2}e}{d-1}=O(\frac{1}{d}) for large dd which improves over the bound Es​q​(αd)=O⁡(log2⁡dd)E_{sq}(\alpha_{d})=O(\frac{\log_{2}d}{d}) which has been obtained using the monogamy of squashed entanglement [19]. Note finally, that the best known lower bound for both EDE_{D} and KDK_{D} is given by 1d\frac{1}{d}. Up to a constant, the bound that we have obtained for squashed entanglement, distillable key (and distillable entanglement, but this we knew before) is therefore optimal. Previously the best known upper bound for distillable key was one half and stems from a computation of the relative entropy of entanglement with respect to separable states (for two copies) of Vollbrecht and Werner who showed that ER,sep​(αd⊗2)≤1−log2⁡d−1dE_{R,\mathrm{sep}}(\alpha_{d}^{\otimes 2})\leq 1-\log_{2}\frac{d-1}{d} [15] and hence ER,sep∞​(αd)≤12​ER,sep​(αd⊗2)≈12+O⁡(1d)E_{R,\mathrm{sep}}^{\infty}(\alpha_{d})\leq\frac{1}{2}E_{R,\mathrm{sep}}(\alpha_{d}^{\otimes 2})\approx\frac{1}{2}+O(\frac{1}{d}). The latter is an upper bound on KDK_{D} [10].

IV Lower bound on the entanglement cost

The calculation of the entanglement cost using its characterisation as the regularised entanglement of formation, equation (8), seems very daunting in general due to the infinite limit; but in fact, even the computation of entanglement of formation according to eq. (7) is a very difficult task. However, for the antisymmetric states αd\alpha_{d} (and many copies thereof), the g⊗gg\otimes g symmetry (for unitary gg) comes to help:

The proof follows by noting that the von Neumann entropy is lower bounded by the quantum collision entropy (or quantum Rényi entropy of order two) H2​(σ)=−log2⁡Tr⁡σ2H_{2}(\sigma)=-\log_{2}\operatorname{Tr}\sigma^{2} and from the formula EC​(ρ)=limn→∞1n​EF​(ρ⊗n)E_{C}(\rho)=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n}E_{F}(\rho^{\otimes n}).   ⊓\sqcap⊔\sqcup

Yura [20] has used this bound to show that the RHS equals 11 if d=3d=3. Together with the observation that the EC​(ρ)≤EF​(ρ)≤2d⁡(d−1)​∑i<jH⁡(ψA,i​j)=1E_{C}(\rho)\leq E_{F}(\rho)\leq\frac{2}{d(d-1)}\sum_{i<j}H(\psi_{A,ij})=1, where |ψi​j⟩=12​(|i​j⟩−|j​i⟩)|\psi_{ij}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|ij\rangle-|ji\rangle), he has thus calculated the entanglement cost of the antisymmetric state in this case. In the following, we will reproduce Yura’s result for d=3d=3 and furthermore show that the RHS is lower bounded by log2⁡43≳0.415\log_{2}\frac{4}{3}\gtrsim 0.415 for all dd.

In order to do so, we will first employ representation theory of the unitary and symmetric group as well as a relaxation in order to reduce the problem to a linear programme. In a second step, we will put a lower bound on the optimal value of this programme using linear programming duality.

In the above formulation we have succeeded to transform the maximisation of the purity of the reduced state over quantum states, which is a quadratic objective function, to a linear optimisation problem over finitely many non-negative real numbers; but with an additional separability constraint. Since this requirement of separability is difficult to handle we will now relax the optimisation problem by only demanding that the state should have a positive partial transpose (PPT).

Since the PPT constraint is a semidefinite constraint, it is clear that we are dealing with a semidefinite programme, and that duality theory should be able to give some information on the maximum value – see a similar line of argument in [16]. We will now show that the right hand side is indeed a linear programme. In order to do so we need to express the PPT condition as a linear constraint in the variables pynp_{y^{n}} and the target function as a linear function in them. This is accomplished by the following lemma.

Now, all that is left to is to find an upper bound on ζn\zeta_{n}, which we obtain by writing down the dual linear programme [17] and guessing a dual feasible point.

Lemma 12

ζn≤(34)n\zeta_{n}\leq(\frac{3}{4})^{n}, hence EF​(αd⊗n)≥n​log2​43E_{F}(\alpha_{d}^{\otimes n})\geq n\log_{2}\frac{4}{3}.

Proof.

The dual linear programme to (17) is given by

where S=T⊤S=T^{\top} and ⊤\top denotes matrix transposition. Its value equals ζn\zeta_{n} by linear programming duality.

In words, a feasible zz in the dual linear programme is an upper bound on all the vector entries of t→⊗n+S⊗n​q→\vec{t}^{\,\otimes n}+S^{\otimes n}\vec{q}. (Caution: some of these may be negative, and so we are not talking about the sup-norm of this vector.) By duality, any such zz is going to be an upper bound on ζn\zeta_{n} [17].

The entries of q→\vec{q} are labelled by strings wn∈{Ψ,Q}nw^{n}\in\{\Psi,Q\}^{n}, and it is clear from the permutation symmetry of the matrix S⊗nS^{\otimes n} and the vector t→⊗n\vec{t}^{\,\otimes n} that we may assume that qwnq_{w^{n}} only depends on the number kk of QQ’s in wnw^{n}:

δk:=wΨn−k​Qk​ and all permutations, for ​k=0,…,n.\delta_{k}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=w_{\Psi^{n-k}Q^{k}}\text{ and all permutations, for }k=0,\ldots,n.

Then, also the constraints in the dual linear programme (18), which are labelled by strings vn∈{0,1}nv^{n}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, depend only on the number mm of 00’s: for each string vn=0m​1n−mv^{n}=0^{m}1^{n-m}, m=0,…,nm=0,\ldots,n, we get an inequality

z≥(−1)m​ 2m−n+∑k=0nδk​∑ℓ=max⁡(0,k+m−n)min⁡(k,m)(−2)ℓ​(mℓ)​(n−mk−ℓ).z\geq(-1)^{m}\,2^{m-n}+\sum_{k=0}^{n}\delta_{k}\sum_{\ell=\max(0,k+m-n)}^{\min(k,m)}(-2)^{\ell}{m\choose\ell}{n-m\choose k-\ell}. (19)

Numerical solutions of the linear programme (18) suggest that in the dual only δ1\delta_{1} is populated and the δj\delta_{j} with j≈nj\approx n. Here we guess a dual feasible solution motivated by this. The ansatz is only an approximation to the numerical findings; for some non-negative β<1\beta<1 and γ\gamma,

δk\displaystyle\delta_{k} =γ​βn−k, for ​k<n\displaystyle=\gamma\beta^{n-k},\ \text{ for }k<n
δn\displaystyle\delta_{n} =0.\displaystyle=0.

Clearly, all δj\delta_{j} are now nonnegative; inserting the above into the dual constraint (19) yields, for all mm, that

z≥(−2)m​2−n+∑k=0nγ​βn−k​∑ℓ=max⁡(0,k+m−n)min⁡(k,m)(−2)ℓ​(mℓ)​(n−mk−ℓ)−γ​(−2)m,z\geq(-2)^{m}2^{-n}+\sum_{k=0}^{n}\gamma\beta^{n-k}\sum_{\ell=\max(0,k+m-n)}^{\min(k,m)}(-2)^{\ell}{m\choose\ell}{n-m\choose k-\ell}-\gamma(-2)^{m},

noticing that the coefficient of the variable αn\alpha_{n} in eq. (19) is (−2)m(-2)^{m}. First we evaluate the double sum; observe that it involves all pairs of kk and ℓ\ell for which the binomial coefficients are nonzero. Hence, it is

∑k,ℓγ​βn−k​(−2)ℓ​(mℓ)​(n−mk−ℓ)=∑k,ℓγ​βn−(k−ℓ)−ℓ​(−2)ℓ​(mℓ)​(n−mk−ℓ)=γ​βn​∑k,ℓ(1β)k−ℓ​(−2β)ℓ​(mℓ)​(n−mk−ℓ)=γ​βn​(1+1β)n−m​(1−2β)m=γ​(β+1)n−m​(β−2)m.\begin{split}\sum_{k,\ell}\gamma\beta^{n-k}(-2)^{\ell}{m\choose\ell}{n-m\choose k-\ell}&=\sum_{k,\ell}\gamma\beta^{n-(k-\ell)-\ell}(-2)^{\ell}{m\choose\ell}{n-m\choose k-\ell}\\ &=\gamma\beta^{n}\sum_{k,\ell}\left(\frac{1}{\beta}\right)^{k-\ell}\left(\frac{-2}{\beta}\right)^{\ell}{m\choose\ell}{n-m\choose k-\ell}\\ &=\gamma\beta^{n}\left(1+\frac{1}{\beta}\right)^{n-m}\left(1-\frac{2}{\beta}\right)^{m}\\ &=\gamma(\beta+1)^{n-m}(\beta-2)^{m}.\end{split}

This simplifies the constraints to

∀mz≥(−2)m​(2−n−γ)+γ​(β+1)n−m​(β−2)m,\forall m\quad z\geq(-2)^{m}\left(2^{-n}-\gamma\right)+\gamma(\beta+1)^{n-m}(\beta-2)^{m},

First of all, the first term can grow very large due to the occurrence of 2m2^{m} – so the only reasonable choice is γ=2−n\gamma=2^{-n}. This reduces the constraints to

In conclusion, we obtain a dual feasible solution with this value, yielding an upper bound ζn≤(3/4)n\zeta_{n}\leq(3/4)^{n}, which gives this as an upper bound on the maximum purity of a reduced state in nn copies of the antisymmetric subspace.   ⊓\sqcap⊔\sqcup

Theorem 2 is now a direct consequence of Lemma 12.

V Regularised Relative Entropy of Entanglement

We start this section by showing that the constant lower bound on the entanglement cost of the antisymmetric state that we have calculated above implies a constant lower bound on the regularised relative entropy of entanglement with respect to separable states, (9). We then show that the regularised relative entropy of entanglement is asymptotically continuous with respect to any convex set of states that contains the maximally mixed state. Examples of such sets are the set of separable states or the set of PPT states.

In contrast, the calculation of [16] gave ER,PPT∞​(αd)=log2⁡d+2dE_{R,\mathrm{PPT}}^{\infty}(\alpha_{d})=\log_{2}\frac{d+2}{d}. This shows, in particular, that ER,PPT∞E_{R,\mathrm{PPT}}^{\infty} differs from ER,sep∞E_{R,\mathrm{sep}}^{\infty} on Werner states. We conclude that squashed entanglement can be much smaller than the regularised relative entropy of entanglement with respect to separable states; the opposite separation was known thanks to the “flower states” of [21].

We close this section by showing the asymptotic continuity of the regularised relative entropy of entanglement.

Proposition 14

The relative entropy of entanglement ER,C∞E^{\infty}_{R,C} with respect to a convex set CC that includes the maximally mixed state, is asymptotically continuous, i.e. there is a function δ⁡(ϵ)\delta(\epsilon) with δ⁡(ϵ)→0\delta(\epsilon)\rightarrow 0 for ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0 such that for all ‖ρ−σ‖1≤ϵ||\rho-\sigma||_{1}\leq\epsilon

|ER,C∞​(ρ)−ER,C∞​(σ)|≤δ⁡(ϵ)​log⁡d,|E^{\infty}_{R,C}(\rho)-E^{\infty}_{R,C}(\sigma)|\leq\delta(\epsilon)\log d,

where dd is the dimension of the system supporting ρ\rho and σ\sigma. In fact the proof shows that δ⁡(ϵ)\delta(\epsilon) can be taken as 2​(ϵ+h​(ϵ))2(\epsilon+h(\epsilon)), where hh denotes the binary entropy function. In particular this proves that ER,sep∞E^{\infty}_{R,\mathrm{sep}} and ER,PPT∞E^{\infty}_{R,\mathrm{PPT}} are asymptotically continuous.

Proof.

Let ‖ρ−σ‖1=ϵ>0\|\rho-\sigma\|_{1}=\epsilon>0, where ρ\rho and σ\sigma are dd-dimensional states. According to Alicki and Fannes [18], there are states γ\gamma, ρ~\tilde{\rho} and σ~\tilde{\sigma} with γ=(1−ϵ)​ρ+ϵ​ρ~=(1−ϵ)​σ+ϵ​σ~\gamma=(1-\epsilon)\rho+\epsilon\tilde{\rho}=(1-\epsilon)\sigma+\epsilon\tilde{\sigma}. If we succeed to prove asymptotic continuity on mixtures, i.e.

|ER,C∞​(ρ)−ER,C∞​(γ)|≤δ⁡(ϵ)2​log⁡d,|E^{\infty}_{R,C}(\rho)-E^{\infty}_{R,C}(\gamma)|\leq\frac{\delta(\epsilon)}{2}\log d, (20)

then continuity for ρ\rho and σ\sigma follows by use of the triangle inequality:

|ER,C∞​(ρ)−ER,C∞​(σ)|≤|ER,C∞​(ρ)−ER,C∞​(γ)|+|ER,C∞​(γ)−ER,C∞​(σ)|≤δ⁡(ϵ)​log⁡d.|E^{\infty}_{R,C}(\rho)-E^{\infty}_{R,C}(\sigma)|\leq|E^{\infty}_{R,C}(\rho)-E^{\infty}_{R,C}(\gamma)|+|E^{\infty}_{R,C}(\gamma)-E^{\infty}_{R,C}(\sigma)|\leq\delta(\epsilon)\log d.

The main step in the proof of the estimate (20) is the following inequality for an ensemble {pi,τi}\{p_{i},\tau_{i}\},

∑ipi​ER,C​(τi)−ER,C​(∑ipi​τi)≤H⁡(∑ipi​τi)−∑ipi​H​(τi)≤H⁡(∑ipi​|i⟩​⟨i|),\sum_{i}p_{i}E_{R,C}(\tau_{i})-E_{R,C}\left(\sum_{i}p_{i}\tau_{i}\right)\leq H\left(\sum_{i}p_{i}\tau_{i}\right)-\sum_{i}p_{i}H(\tau_{i})\leq H\left(\sum_{i}p_{i}|i\rangle\!\langle i|\right), (21)

where |i⟩|i\rangle denotes an orthonormal basis. Inequality (21) has first been proven for the relative entropy with respect to the set of separable states [22] (see also [23]) and then been extended to hold for any convex set that includes the maximally mixed state [24]. Here, it implies the following estimate

ER,C​(γ⊗N)≥∑kϵk​(1−ϵ)N−k​(Nk)​ER,C​(ρ⊗(N−k)⊗ρ~⊗k)−N​h​(ϵ),E_{R,C}(\gamma^{\otimes N})\geq\sum_{k}\epsilon^{k}(1-\epsilon)^{N-k}\binom{N}{k}E_{R,C}(\rho^{\otimes(N-k)}\otimes\tilde{\rho}^{\otimes k})-Nh(\epsilon),

where h⁡(ϵ)h(\epsilon) is the Shannon entropy of the distribution (ϵ,1−ϵ)(\epsilon,1-\epsilon). We will now replace all ρ~\tilde{\rho}’s on the RHS by ρ\rho’s. This is done in two steps: i) remove the states of the form ρ~\tilde{\rho} on the RHS, since the partial trace operations is an LOCC operation the RHS can only decrease, ii) append the states ρ\rho and apply the inequality

ER,C​(ρ⊗N)≤ER,C​(ρ⊗(N−k))+k​ER,C​(ρ),E_{R,C}(\rho^{\otimes N})\leq E_{R,C}(\rho^{\otimes(N-k)})+kE_{R,C}(\rho),

which holds by subadditivity of ER,CE_{R,C}. This gives

This concludes the proof of the estimate (20) and the proposition.   ⊓\sqcap⊔\sqcup

A vital ingredient in the proof was inequality (21), which bounds the strength of the convexity of the relative entropy. Prior to this work, the same inequality has been used in [26] to prove that the relative entropy of entanglement cannot be locked. As both entanglement of purification and formation are lockable, a simple translation of inequality (21) to these measures is not possible. Other ways to verify that entanglement cost under LOCC and LOq (local operations with a sublinear amount of quantum communication) are asymptotically continuous will have to be found.

VI Conclusion

We have shown a way of – in principle – calculating the Rényi-2 entropic version of the entanglement of cost of the d×dd\times d-antisymmetric state via convex optimisation and more specifically, semidefinite programming. Using a linear programming relaxation we showed a constant lower bound, independent of dd. Tighter relaxations are possible, in principle capable of obtaining the exact value of the maximum purity of the reduced state over all |ψ⟩∈                             ⊗n|\psi\rangle\in{\,\hskip 0.0pt\vbox{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=2.72pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.67998pt\hbox to3.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=2.72pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.67998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=2.72pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.67998pt\hbox to3.4pt{\hfil}\vrule height=2.72pt,width=0.3pt,depth=0.67998pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}^{\otimes n}: in addition to the PPT condition of the state between A​BAB and A′​B′A^{\prime}B^{\prime}, we should impose that the state is shareable (or extendible) to more parties [27, 28, 29, 30, 31]. At the same time, we could show that the squashed entanglement of these states is asymptotically small, implying that also their distillable key is asymptotically small.

We believe that our result is the strongest indication so far that “quantum bound key” exists: states with positive key cost to create them (a notion not yet defined in the literature, and a little tricky to formalize cleanly), while their distillable key is zero. At least we show that the states have asymptotically vanishing distillable key (it cannot be zero, as a lower bound of Ω⁡(1d)\Omega(\frac{1}{d}) on EDE_{D} is known); on the other hand, their entanglement cost does not vanish.

The technique to obtain the lower bound on EC​(αd)E_{C}(\alpha_{d}) is yet another demonstration of the power of symmetry in entanglement theory. But to our knowledge, it is the first application of plethysms in this field. Unfortunately, we do not prove the conjectured EC​(αd)=1E_{C}(\alpha_{d})=1; our PPT relaxation cannot give anything better than ≈0.45\approx 0.45 as computer solutions of the linear programme up to n=12n=12 show (see Appendix). It remains to be investigated whether further constraints, for instance of shareability, can improve the lower bound to 11 — or whether indeed EC​(αd)<1E_{C}(\alpha_{d})<1 which would provide an explicit counterexample to additivity.

In comparison to the large gap observed between the entanglement of formation and distillable key [32], our work exhibits three advantages. Firstly, our example is constructive, secondly, we show that the distillable key can be made arbitrarily small and thirdly, we consider the entanglement cost, which is the right measure to compare with the distillable key, and which can be strictly smaller than the entanglement of formation [13]. The distinction between entanglement cost and entanglement of formation is crucial here, as it was for the discovery of bound entanglement [33], since the asymptotic measure of distillable key has to be compared to an asymptotic measure of preparing the state. A further result in [32] shows that the one-way distillable key is generically small, even if entanglement of formation is large. In our work, in contrast, the one-way distillable key of the antisymmetric state αd\alpha_{d} vanishes for all d≥3d\geq 3.

Our results can readily be generalised to the multiparty entanglement of the state proportional to the antisymmetric projector onto several parties. The multiparty squashed entanglement and distillable key [34] exhibit a behaviour similar to the two-party case. Due to the difficulty of classifying multiparty entanglement, it is not clear which multiparty generalisation of entanglement cost to use. Any such generalisation, however, should be larger than entanglement cost of the two-party state, to which our lower bound applies.

Due to the partial transpose we have to deal with decomposing tensor products that involve dual representations. In order to be able to continue to use the Young frame notation (rather than the highest weight notation) in this situation, we use S​U​(d)SU(d) rather than U⁡(d)U(d). The action of S​U​(d)SU(d) on ∧d(𝐂d)\wedge^{d}(\mathbf{C}^{d}) is namely trivial and allows us therefore to add full columns and convert negative weights into positive ones. For the spaces, this difference is immaterial and therefore of no concern to us.
